summary: Defines two new IPv4 Options used only with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: ILNP gives every node a permanent 64-bit name and separate addresses that reach it. IPv4 headers have no space for such a name, so RFC 6746 puts it in a header option instead. A second option carries a random number that only the real sender could know, which lets a receiver tell a genuine message from a forged one.

questions: what ip options does ilnp use
what are the two ilnpv4 ipv4 options
how does ilnpv4 carry identifiers in ipv4
why use ipv4 options instead of extension headers
subtitle: IPv4 header options that carry ILNP identifiers and nonces for security.

tldr.problem: ILNP for IPv4 needs to carry 64-bit node identifiers in packets, but the IPv4 header has no room for them. It also needs a security nonce to stop off-path attackers forging ILNP messages.
tldr.mechanism: Two new IPv4 options using the same experimental option number, 158, carry the identifier values and a cryptographically random 64-bit nonce. Each option is marked to be copied on fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: This proposal lets ILNPv4 work much as ILNPv6 does, but using IPv4's option mechanism rather than extension headers, because router hardware can already parse past IPv4 options.

facts.label: ILNPv4_OPT values
facts.value: 0x01 for the identifier, 0x02 for the nonce

today: RFC 6746 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is part of the ILNP set from the IRTF Routing Research Group, alongside the architecture in RFC 6740, the engineering considerations in RFC 6741 and the locator update messages in RFC 6743 and RFC 6745. Like the rest of the set, it is a research proposal rather than a deployed protocol.

sections.title: Why ILNP Needs Two IPv4 Options
sections.content:
ILNP differs from the current Internet architecture primarily by deprecating the concept of an IP address and defining two new objects with crisp syntax and semantics. The first is the Locator, a topology-dependent name for a subnetwork. The second is the Identifier, a topology-independent name for a node.

ILNP has more than one possible engineering instantiation, and this document covers ILNPv4, the instance based on and backwards compatible with IPv4. As with ILNPv6, when ILNPv4 is used for a network-layer session, the upper-layer protocols, such as the TCP and UDP pseudo-header checksum and the IPsec security association, bind only to the identifiers and never to the locators. Only the locator values are used for routing and forwarding ILNPv4 packets.

This document defines two new IPv4 options: an Identifier option and a Nonce option. The nonce option does for ILNPv4 what the IPv6 Nonce Destination Option does for ILNPv6, which is to prevent off-path attacks against ILNP ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: ILNP splits a node's name from the addresses that reach it. The name is fixed and the addresses change. This memo is about how an IPv4 packet carries that name.

sections.title: One Option Number, Two Options
sections.content:
Both options are control options, so they use IPv4 Option Class 0, and both must be copied when a packet is fragmented.

The two options were originally specified to use separate option numbers. Only one IPv4 option number, decimal 158, has been defined for experimental use with the properties of MUST COPY and CONTROL, so the two options were reworked to share it. To tell them apart, an unsigned 8-bit field called ILNPv4_OPT inside the option is examined: the value 0x01 marks the Identifier option and the value 0x02 marks the Nonce option.

The memo warns implementers that option number 158 is not uniquely allocated to ILNPv4. Other IPv4 experiments might be using the same option value for different options with different formats, so a node that meets this option has to check the ILNPv4_OPT field before treating it as an ILNP option.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one experimental option number was free, so both options share it and carry a small tag that says which one they are. A node has to read that tag, because other experiments may use the same number for something else entirely.

sections.title: The ILNPv4 Packet Format
sections.content:
In an ILNPv4 packet the source IP address in the IPv4 header becomes the source ILNPv4 locator value and the destination IP address becomes the destination locator value. Backwards compatibility requires that ILNPv4 locators use the same number space as IPv4 routing prefixes.

ILNPv4 uses the same 64-bit identifier, with the same modified EUI-64 syntax, as ILNPv6. Because the IPv4 address fields are much smaller than the IPv6 ones, ILNPv4 cannot carry the identifier values in the fixed portion of the IPv4 header. There are two obvious ways to carry them: as an IPv4 option, or as an IPv6-style extension header placed after the IPv4 header and before the upper-layer protocol.

The memo gives a hardware reason for choosing the option. Currently deployed IPv4 routers from multiple vendors use packet forwarding silicon that can parse past IPv4 options to examine the upper-layer protocol header at wire speed on reasonably fast interfaces, of 1 Gbps or better. No existing IPv4-capable forwarding silicon can parse past a new extension header for IPv4. So ILNPv4 uses a new IPv4 option to carry the identifier values, and a second new option carries the nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP addresses in the header act as locators, and the node's own name rides along in an option. An extension header would have been the tidier design, but the chips in today's routers cannot read past one at speed, so the option is the practical choice.

sections.title: The Identifier Option and the Nonce Option
sections.content:
The Identifier option is 20 octets long, which is 5 words: a four-octet header holding the option type, the option length, a zero octet and the ILNPv4_OPT value, followed by the source identifier and the destination identifier as unsigned 64-bit integers. RFC 6741 specifies the syntax, the semantics and the generation of ILNP identifier values, and using the same syntax for every instantiation of ILNP simplifies specification and implementation and makes a future translation between ILNPv4 and ILNPv6 easier.

This option must not be present in an IPv4 packet unless the packet is part of an ILNPv4 session. An ILNPv4 session must include it in the first few packets, and may include it in all packets of the session. It is recommended to include it in all packets when packet loss is higher than normal.

The Nonce option holds a four-octet header of the same shape, with the ILNPv4_OPT value 0x02, followed by a 64-bit nonce. All ILNP nonce values are unidirectional, so when TCP is in use the underlying session has two different nonce values, one from initiator to responder and another from responder to initiator. The nonce gives non-cryptographic protection against off-path attacks, such as forged ICMP messages from the far end of a TCP session. Each nonce value must be unpredictable, that is, cryptographically random, with guidance in RFC 4086. The option must not appear outside an ILNPv4 session, must be included in the first few packets of each session, must be included in all ICMP messages generated by endpoints taking part in an ILNP session, and may be included in all packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier option carries the two 64-bit names, and the nonce option carries a random number. The random number must be different in each direction and must be impossible to guess, because it is what proves a message came from the node it claims to come from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the overall ILNP architecture are in RFC 6740 and the common ones in RFC 6741.

If the ILNP nonce value is predictable, an off-path attacker might be able to forge data or control packets. The memo says this risk is also mitigated by the common practice of IP source address filtering.

IP Security for ILNP provides cryptographic protection for ILNP data and control packets, but the ILNP nonce option is required in any case, even when IPsec is in use. Deployments of ILNPv4 in high-threat environments should use IPsec as well, for additional risk reduction.
sections.plainLanguage: The random number stops a stranger forging messages. Encryption is still worth adding on links where the traffic is sensitive, but the random number is needed either way.

fields.name: Option Type
fields.desc: 158, the experimental option number shared by both ILNP options.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: The length of the option in words.

fields.name: ILNPv4_OPT
fields.desc: 0x01 identifies this as the Identifier option.

fields.name: Source Identifier
fields.desc: The 64-bit identifier of the sending node.

fields.name: Destination Identifier
fields.desc: The 64-bit identifier of the receiving node.

fields.name: Option Type
fields.desc: 158, the experimental option number shared by both ILNP options.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: The length of the option in words.

fields.name: ILNPv4_OPT
fields.desc: 0x02 identifies this as the Nonce option.

fields.name: Nonce
fields.desc: The 64-bit nonce. It must be cryptographically random, and each direction of a session has its own value.

viz.caption: RULES THAT APPLY TO BOTH ILNPv4 OPTIONS

items.title: Copied on fragmentation
items.text: Both options are marked to be copied when a packet is fragmented.

items.title: Control class
items.text: Both use IPv4 Option Class 0, which carries control information.

items.title: Shared number
items.text: Both use option number 158, which is not uniquely allocated to ILNPv4.

items.title: Session only
items.text: Neither option may appear in a packet that is not part of an ILNPv4 session.
